title: Festive nebulae
caption: The nebula NGC 248 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 248 · constellation Tucana · about 200000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, K. Sandstrom (University of California, San Diego), and the SMIDGE team.

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This glowing nebula is NGC 248, which lies inside the Small Magellanic Cloud, a companion galaxy of the Milky Way roughly 200,000 light-years from Earth. Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed it in September 2015.

NGC 248 is an emission nebula, a cloud of gas that shines on its own. In such nebulae, hot stars typically flood the gas with energetic light, which strips electrons from hydrogen atoms. As the atoms recapture them, the gas gives off light of its own, especially in the red glow of hydrogen.

The observations were part of a survey nicknamed SMIDGE. Its full title spells out its purpose, which is to investigate how dust and gas evolve in the Small Magellanic Cloud. NGC 248 was one of the targets Hubble looked at for that project, using its Advanced Camera for Surveys.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.22 x 2.22 arcminutes) and distance (200000 light years), the frame spans roughly 129 × 129 light-years. Its light set out about 200,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the nebula in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter and long exposures reveal a glow far too faint for the eye to see at this distance.
